q: What is the general chemical formula of a perovskite?
explain: Perovskites follow ABX₃: a large A-site cation, a smaller B-site cation inside an octahedron of X anions (usually oxygen or a halide). This simple formula hides enormous chemical flexibility.

q: The Goldschmidt tolerance factor t ≈ 1 indicates what about a perovskite?
options: An ideal cubic structure is likely stable
explain: t = (r_A + r_X) / √2(r_B + r_X). Near t = 1, the ions pack into the ideal cubic perovskite. Between ~0.8–1.0 distorted variants form — and those distortions are themselves a powerful design tool.

q: During discharge of a zinc–air battery, which reaction occurs at the air cathode?
explain: On discharge, atmospheric O₂ is reduced at the air cathode (ORR) while zinc oxidizes at the anode. On charge the cathode reverses to OER — which is why bifunctional catalysts like doped perovskites are so valuable.

options: It is produced by water electrolysis powered by renewable electricity
It is stored in green pressurized cylinders
It comes from natural gas with carbon capture
explain: Colour labels track the production route: green = renewable-powered electrolysis, grey = steam methane reforming without capture, blue = fossil-based with carbon capture. Only green hydrogen is near-zero carbon at source.

q: The minimum thermodynamic voltage required to split water into H₂ and O₂ is:
explain: ΔG = 237 kJ/mol for water splitting gives E = ΔG/nF = 1.23 V at 25 °C. Real electrolyzers need more — the extra voltage is the 'overpotential', and reducing it is the central mission of electrocatalysis.

options: Extra voltage beyond the thermodynamic value needed to drive a reaction at a useful rate
The maximum voltage a battery can deliver
Voltage lost to wiring resistance only
The open-circuit voltage of a cell
explain: Kinetics charge a toll: sluggish electron transfer and gas evolution demand voltage beyond the thermodynamic 1.23 V (for water splitting). A great catalyst is one that shrinks this toll.

q: The CISS effect — central to chiral electrocatalysis — stands for:
explain: Chiral molecules and surfaces preferentially transmit electrons of one spin orientation. In water splitting, spin-polarized electrons favour the desired O₂ (triplet) pathway — boosting efficiency and suppressing side products like H₂O₂.

q: X-ray diffraction (XRD) identifies crystal structures using which law?
explain: X-rays reflecting off parallel atomic planes interfere constructively when nλ = 2d·sinθ. The resulting peak pattern is a fingerprint of the lattice — the first thing a materials scientist checks after synthesis.

q: Oxygen vacancies in perovskite oxides typically:
options: Can enhance catalytic activity and ionic conductivity
explain: Vacancies alter the B-site oxidation state and create active surface sites for oxygen chemistry. Deliberate defect engineering — imperfection by design — is how modern perovskite catalysts are tuned.

q: Which of these is NOT a perovskite?
explain: Rutile TiO₂ has formula AX₂ with a different octahedral network. SrTiO₃, BaTiO₃, and LaMnO₃ are all classic ABO₃ perovskites — spanning dielectrics, ferroelectrics, and magnetism in one structural family.

q: The key difference between SEM and TEM microscopy is:
options: TEM transmits electrons through an ultra-thin sample, achieving far higher resolution
SEM uses light instead of electrons
explain: SEM scans a surface with a focused beam (topography, ~nm resolution); TEM shoots electrons through a sample thinned to <100 nm, resolving atomic columns. Choosing between them is choosing between skin and skeleton.

q: In ABO₃ perovskite electrocatalysts, which site usually governs catalytic activity?
explain: The B-site transition metal's d-electron configuration (e.g., the eg occupancy descriptor) largely sets how reaction intermediates bind. A-site substitution is often used indirectly — to tune the B-site's oxidation state.

q: DFT, the workhorse of computational materials science, stands for:
explain: DFT computes a material's electronic structure from its electron density rather than the many-body wavefunction — making quantum mechanics tractable enough to screen thousands of candidate materials before anyone enters a lab.

options: Steam methane reforming without carbon capture
explain: Over 90% of today's hydrogen is grey: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂, emitting ~9–10 kg CO₂ per kg H₂. Replacing it with green hydrogen is one of the largest decarbonization opportunities on Earth.

q: Why do zinc–air batteries offer such high theoretical energy density?
options: One reactant (oxygen) comes free from the surrounding air
They operate at very high voltage
explain: The cathode's active material — oxygen — isn't carried inside the cell; it's breathed from air. Removing that mass from the package gives zinc–air a theoretical energy density (~1,086 Wh/kg) several times that of Li-ion.
